vo.text: In 1066, England had three kings in a single year. This is the battle that decided the last one.
In January, the old king died. The English crowned a powerful lord named Harold.
Across the sea, in Normandy, a duke named William said: excuse me, that crown was promised to me. And he built a fleet to come and get it.
But first, a Viking king, Harald Hardrada, invaded the north. Harold marched up and beat him, at Stamford Bridge.
Three days later, William landed in the south. So Harold marched his tired army all the way back down. About two hundred and fifty miles. Busy month.
On the fourteenth of October, Harold's army stood on top of a hill. Shoulder to shoulder. Shields locked together into a wall.
William's army waited at the bottom. Archers, foot soldiers, and knights on horseback. Their job: go up the hill. Not fun.
The Normans attacked. Arrows thudded into the shields. Knights rode uphill into swinging axes. And the shield wall held. Hour after hour.
Then a rumour ran through the Norman lines: William is dead! His soldiers started to run.
William pushed back his helmet so everyone could see his face. I'm alive! And he turned them around.
Then, the Norman writers say, they tried a trick. They pretended to run away.
Some of the English chased them down the hill. And the moment they left the wall, the Norman knights turned and surrounded them.
They did it more than once. And with every chase, the shield wall got thinner.
Late in the day, King Harold was killed. A famous embroidery, the Bayeux Tapestry, may show him with an arrow in his eye. Historians still argue about it. It is very hard to ask a tapestry questions.
Without their king, the English army broke apart.
On Christmas Day, William was crowned King of England. We still call him William the Conqueror.
His Normans spoke French. Which is why English today has words like beef, jury and judge. All thanks to one very long afternoon on a hill.
